taxonomy.subtopic: Lead-time bias and survival measured from an earlier diagnosis

questions.stem_html: A cancer-screening program detects tumors at a mean age of 62 years. In a comparable unscreened population, the same tumors are diagnosed after symptoms develop at a mean age of 67 years. In both groups, the mean age at cancer-related death is 70 years, but survival measured from diagnosis appears longer in the screened group. Which phenomenon best explains the apparent benefit?
questions.explanation_html: Screening advances the date of diagnosis without changing the date of death. Measuring survival from the earlier diagnosis therefore creates an artificial increase in observed survival even though no life has been prolonged. Disease-specific mortality, rather than survival time from diagnosis, is needed to assess whether screening truly reduces deaths.

wrong_choice_explanations.2: Length bias occurs because periodic screening preferentially detects slower-growing disease with a longer preclinical phase; the scenario instead holds the death date constant and changes only the diagnosis date.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Recall bias results from differential accuracy of remembered prior exposures and is not the mechanism shown.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Berkson bias is a selection bias arising from hospital-based sampling when admission is related to both exposure and disease.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Confounding by indication occurs when the reason a treatment is selected is itself related to outcome.

questions.educational_objective: Lead-time bias falsely lengthens survival measured from diagnosis when screening moves diagnosis earlier but does not delay death.

media.alt_text: Original paired timeline showing earlier screen detection but the same date of cancer-related death in screened and unscreened groups.
